rows.acip: LAM DMAN PA NYAN RANG LAS KHYAD PAR DU BYED PA SEMS BSKYED KYI KHRID LA, SEMS BSKYED 'DI GAL SHIN TU CHE BA, LAM RIM CHEN MO LAS, CHOS THEG PA CHEN PO'I CHOS YIN PAS MI CHOG ,GANG ZAG THEG PA CHEN PO BAR 'GRO DGOS GSUNGS PA LTAR BYANG CHUB KYI SEMS KYI RTZIS ZIN NA BYED RGYU THEG DMAN GYI CHOS YIN YANG THEG PA CHEN POR 'GRO,
rows.wylie: lam dman pa nyan rang las khyad par du byed pa sems bskyed kyi khrid la, sems bskyed 'di gal shin tu che ba, lam rim chen mo las, chos theg pa chen po'i chos yin pas mi chog ,gang zag theg pa chen po bar 'gro dgos gsungs pa ltar byang chub kyi sems kyi rtsis zin na byed rgyu theg dman gyi chos yin yang theg pa chen por 'gro
rows.english: What distinguishes this practice from the lower paths, those of the listeners and self-made buddhas, is the teaching on the Wish to achieve Buddhahood.  The Wish is absolutely vital.  As the Greater Steps on the Path states, "It's not enough for his Dharma to be the Dharma of the greater way.  The person who practices it has to be a person of the greater way."  We may even be practicing the Dharma of the lower way, but it turns to the Dharma of the higher way, if our hearts are imbued by this Wish for Buddhahood.

rows.acip: DE NAS BLA MA'I RNAL 'BYOR GYI BLA MA RNAMS KYI MDUN DU STON PA THUB PA'I DBANG PO LA 'GRO BA KUN GYIS SRI ZHU BYA BA'I 'OS SU GYUR PA DKON MCHOG SRI ZHU'I MGRON RGYUD SDE BZHI'I YI DAM, LONGS SPRUL GYI SANGS RGYAS, DE DAG GIS GSUNGS PA'I LUNG RTOGS KYI CHOS PO TI'I RNAM PA CAN, DE NYAMS SU LEN PA'I DGE 'DUN BYANG SEMS NYAN RANG RNAMS KYIS BSKOR BA,
rows.wylie: de nas bla ma'i rnal 'byor gyi bla ma rnams kyi mdun du ston pa thub pa'i dbang po la 'gro ba kun gyis sri zhu bya ba'i 'os su gyur pa dkon mchog sri zhu'i mgron rgyud sde bzhi'i yi dam, longs sprul gyi sangs rgyas, de dag gis gsungs pa'i lung rtogs kyi chos po ti'i rnam pa can, de nyams su len pa'i dge 'dun byang sems nyan rang rnams kyis bskor ba
rows.english: Next we visualize the Teacher, the Lord of the Able Ones, in front of the Lamas we have invited for the Practice of the Lama.  Surrounding Him are all the precious Jewels, the beings that we call the "Guests of Holy Service," for they are worthy objects of the holy service of all living kind. These guests include the Close Angels of all four secret groups; the Enjoyment and Emanation Bodies of the Buddhas; the Teachings they have spoken, both the physical Word and the realizations brought about by the Word, all in the form of volumes of scripture; and the spiritual community who puts these teachings into practice: Bodhisattvas, listeners, and self-made buddhas.

rows.acip: CHOS 'BYUNG DBUS RNAL 'BYOR MA, DE'I MTHAR 'KHOR BZHI, DE'I MTHAR 'KHOR SO GNYIS, DE'I MTHAR RGYUD SDE BZHI'I YI DAM SANGS RGYAS BYANG SEMS NYAN RANG BCAS DANG,

rows.english: Here your Root and Lineage Lamas are above, in space.  At the center of the dharma star* is the Holy Angel; around Her are the retinue of four, and around Them are the retinue of thirty-two.  Around Them are all the Close Angels, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Listeners, and Self-Made Buddhas of all the four groups of the secret teachings. * The Tibetan editor notes a possible error here.

rows.acip: 'BUL SNGAGS DANG POS BLA MA YI DAM SANGS RGYAS BYANG SEMS NYAN RANG BCAS DANG, GNYIS PAS MDUN RGYAB KYI MKHA' 'GRO CHOS SRUNG, GSUM PAS MTHA' SKOR GYI MGRON RNAMS LA 'BUL DGOS GSUNGS,
rows.wylie: 'bul sngags dang pos bla ma yi dam sangs rgyas byang sems nyan rang bcas dang, gnyis pas mdun rgyab kyi mkha' 'gro chos srung, gsum pas mtha' skor gyi mgron rnams la 'bul dgos gsungs
rows.english: With the first repetition of the secret words of offering, said our Lama, you must present the torma to the Lamas, Close Angels, Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Listeners, and Self-Made Buddhas.  With the second repetition you offer it to the Angels and Protectors of the Dharma who are located in the front and back.  And in the third repetition you are presenting it to the guests of the circle beyond these. The Practice of Acting Left-Ways

rows.acip: DE'I STENG GI BAR SNANG NGAM RIGS BDAG GI THUGS KAR RTZA BRGYUD KYI BLA MA, RNAL 'BYOR MA'I MTHA' SKOR DU 'KHOR BZHI, DE'I MTHAR 'KHOR SO GNYIS, DE'I MTHAR RGYUD SDE BZHI'I YI DAM, SANGS RGYAS, BYANG SEMS, NYAN RANG RNAMS DANG,

rows.english: In the air above Her--or else within the holy heart of the Lord of Enlightened Kind--are your root and lineage Lamas.  Circling the Holy Angel are the four Ladies of Her retinue.  Forming another ring outside them are the retinue of the 32 Angels.  And in another ring outside Them are the Close Angels of the four groups of the secret teachings; Buddhas; bodhisattvas; and enemy destroyers of the Listener and Self-Made Buddha tracks.

rows.acip: GTZO MO'I STENG DU RTZA BRGYUD KYI BLA MA RNAMS DANG, MTHA' SKOR DU RNAL 'BYOR MA SO GNYIS SOGS YI DAM SANGS RGYAS BYANG SEMS NYAN RANG,

rows.english: Atop the central Angel then we would see our root and lineage Lamas; and all around the 32 Angels and so on: close Angels, Buddhas, bodhisattvas, listeners and self-made Buddhas.

rows.acip: CES PA STE, 'DI LA MTHUN MONG MA YIN PA'I SNGON 'GRO BZHI ZHES KYANG GSUNGS LA, DE YANG LAM LOG PA MU STEGS BYED LAS KHYAD PAR DU BYED PA SKYABS 'GRO'I 'KHRID, LAM DMAN PA NYAN RANG LAS KHYAD PAR DU BYED PA SEMS BSKYED KYI 'KHRID, SDIG SGRIB DAG PAR BYED PA RDOR SEMS SGOM BZLAS KYI 'KHRID, BYIN RLABS 'JUG PAR BYED PA BLA MA'I RNAL 'BYOR GYI 'KHRID RNAMS YIN PAS DANG PO GNYIS DANG BZHI PA TSAD MED KYI RNAL 'BYOR DON GCIG STE,
rows.wylie: ces pa ste, 'di la mthun mong ma yin pa'i sngon 'gro bzhi zhes kyang gsungs la, de yang lam log pa mu stegs byed las khyad par du byed pa skyabs 'gro'i 'khrid, lam dman pa nyan rang las khyad par du byed pa sems bskyed kyi 'khrid, sdig sgrib dag par byed pa rdor sems sgom bzlas kyi 'khrid, byin rlabs 'jug par byed pa bla ma'i rnal 'byor gyi 'khrid rnams yin pas dang po gnyis dang bzhi pa tshad med kyi rnal 'byor don gcig ste
rows.english: These are known as the four unique preliminaries.  Now the teachings on going for refuge are what distinguish the Buddhist path from mistaken paths of non-Buddhists.  The teachings on developing the Wish for enlightenment are what set this path apart from the two lower Buddhist paths of the listeners and self-realized ones.  The teachings on meditation and recitation of the Warrior of Diamond act to purify us of our negative actions and our obstacles.  And the teachings on the practice of the Lama allow us to receive the Lama's blessing.  Thus the first, second, and fourth of these are all considered the single deep practice of the limitless.

rows.acip: G-YON 'DAB TU RJE BTZUN 'JAM DBYANGS LA MDO PHYOGS KYI DGE 'DUN BYANG SEMS NYAN RANG DANG SNGAGS PHYOGS KYI DGE 'DUN DPA' BO MKHA' 'GRO,
rows.wylie: g-yon 'dab tu rje btsun 'jam dbyangs la mdo phyogs kyi dge 'dun byang sems nyan rang dang sngags phyogs kyi dge 'dun dpa' bo mkha' 'gro
rows.english: On the petal to their left21 is the holy Manjushri, together with all the community of the open teachings--the bodhisattvas, listeners, and self-realized ones; and the community of the secret teachings as well--the Warriors and their Angels.

rows.acip: RIM PA BZHIN DU NYAN RANG GI RIGS CAN LA CHAGS BRAL GYI SPYOD PA DANG, PHAR PHYIN THEG PA'I GDUL BYA LA SA DANG PHA ROL TU PHYIN PA'I SPYOD PA DANG, SNGAGS GYI GDUL BYA LA 'DOD CHAGS KYI SPYOD PA BSTAN PA'I PHYIR,

rows.english: This is the case because they have taught, respectively, the activities which do not involve using desire to those who belong to the category of listeners and self-made Buddhas; the activities relating to the bodhisattva levels and perfections to disciples who belong to the open way of the perfections; and the activities which do involve using desire to disciples of the way of the secret word.

rows.english: Training oneself in the method side of things, in the widespread side, is moreover not something that we find in the paths of the listeners and the self-made buddhas.  Nor do we find there any of the subjects relating to using simultaneous bliss to meditate upon emptiness.  Since followers of these systems then acquaint themselves primarily with the deep practice of emptiness, they are described as "incomplete," as "leaving us, in the way a butter lamp does."

rows.wylie: gnyis pa spyan 'dren rgyas par bshad pa ni, phun tshogs bde legs 'byung gnas sogs rkang pa bzhi gsungs te, (phun) sum (tshogs) pa mngon mtho lha mi'i (bde) ba dang, nges par (legs) pa nyan rang sangs rgyas kyi byang chub gsum gyis bsdus pa'i legs tshogs ma lus pa 'byung ba'i (gnas) sam gzhi
rows.english: This brings us to our second part, a more detailed explanation of how we call down the Beings of Wisdom.  This is presented in the nine lines that begin with "Come my root and lineage Lamas..."  Our root and lineage Lamas are here being described as the true source, or foundation, from which each and every good thing that ever happens to us comes.  These include perfect happiness--which here refers to the happiness of the higher rebirths, among worldly gods, and humans; as well as definite goodness, a reference to the three types of enlightenment: those of the listener, the self-made buddha, and the true Buddha.

rows.english: To win freedom you must eliminate, from its root, this grasping to a "self." To eliminate it, you must meditate on how nothing has a self: you must find a path or mental viewpoint which holds things in a way that is completely incompatible with the way you now grasp for a "self." You can make any great efforts you want in practices like charity and morality, but without this meditation on no-self you will never be able to attain freedom. As the 400 Verses says, "There is no second door to peace."146 This wisdom which perceives that no self exists is then a "without which nothing" for freeing yourself from the circle of life.

rows.english: You see then that interdependence is infallible, that it is nothing but using a concept to label the collection of parts that serve as the basis to take our label. Just seeing this fact, that interdependence never fails, brings you a realization that completely obviates the way that your tendency to grasp to true existence holds its objects. And then when you think of emptiness, you see interdependence; when you think of interdependence, you see emptiness. This is by the way what certain holy sages have meant when they said, "Once you grasp the secret of interdependence, the meaning of emptiness comes in a flash."167

rows.english: That state of mind which acts to establish the existence of physical form and other such things, and which is colored by seeing things as being real, and which is not affected by a temporary factor that would cause it to be mistaken, is only the deceptive mind. This deceptive state of mind though is not the actual grasping to real existence, for it holds its object in a way which is consistent with what the object actually is. The state of mind is deceptive in that the deceptive mind is affected by the tendency to grasp to things as being real.

rows.english: Let us first consider enemy destroyers of the Listener or Self-Made Buddha type. Aren't you saying then that, like the non-Buddhists, they fail to eliminate all the widespread mental afflictions that operate in all three realms? Because isn't it true that they have failed to achieve the path which is directly incompatible, in the way it holds its object, with the root of all these afflictions; that is, the tendency to conceive of things as existing through some nature of their own? And this is true, for they lack that comprehensive knowledge where they realize that things have no nature of their own.

rows.english: Here is the first point, which is establishing that patience is easy to rely upon once you have accustomed yourself to it. If you make a habit of patience, then you will be able to endure any kind of suffering. The way we think of anything is based primarily on how we have become accustomed to think, on our mental habits. As such there is nothing in the world--that is, no quality of the mind--which does not come easily if you make a habit of it.

rows.acip: ,BLTOS DANG MI BLTOS DNGOS 'GAL DANG, ,KHYOD KYI BLO DANG NGA YI BLO, ,'DZIN STANGS DNGOS 'GAL ZHUGS PA YIN, ,TSA GRANG LTA BUR 'GAL BA YIN,
rows.wylie: bltos dang mi bltos dngos 'gal dang, ,khyod kyi blo dang nga yi blo, ,'dzin stangs dngos 'gal zhugs pa yin, ,tsha grang lta bur 'gal ba yin
rows.english: It's impossible for a single thing To depend on other things and also not Depend on them, at the very same time. The way you think of things, And the way I think of things, Are two incompatible things, Like a single thing hot and cold. In short, it's impossible for the pen to come from me, and not come from me, both at the same time.  The way the Devil sees things and the way the Angel sees things will forever be mutually incompatible.  Again, one of us must leave the mind, forever.

rows.acip: ,BONG BU ZHON NAS BONG BU 'TSOL, ,KHYOD NI SKYES PA KHO NAS NI, ,'DI RU SDOD PA 'DZIN STANGS 'GAL,
rows.wylie: bong bu zhon nas bong bu 'tshol, ,khyod ni skyes pa kho nas ni, ,'di ru sdod pa 'dzin stangs 'gal
rows.english: You're riding out on the donkey To look for the donkey you lost! The very fact that you've popped up Here within the mind Is what makes it impossible For you to stay: The way that you and I see things Is completely incompatible. The reference to the donkey goes back to the story of a nomad who had a herd of fifty donkeys that he would let out onto a grassy hillside in the morning, and then go round them up and return them to the stables at night.  One unaware day he rode out to collect the herd and as he counted, kept coming up with only 49 present. Yes, he was forgetting to count donkey #50—the one that he was riding on! The point here is that the development of wisdom in our mind must be very careful and purposeful; just waiting for a lucky “wisdom moment” is not going to be enough to stop millions of years of mistaken perceptual habits.  We need to commit ourselves to the task of mastering wisdom, and give it a good block of time every day—through study and meditation.

rows.acip: ,DES NA KHYOD DANG NGA GNYIS NI, ,'DZIN STANGS DNGOS 'GAL ZHUGS PA 'DIS, ,LHAN CIG SDOD PA'I GNAS MA MCHIS, ,KHYOD RANG 'GRO BA'I GNAS LA RGYUG
rows.wylie: des na khyod dang nga gnyis ni, ,'dzin stangs dngos 'gal zhugs pa 'dis, ,lhan cig sdod pa'i gnas ma mchis, ,khyod rang 'gro ba'i gnas la rgyug
rows.english: Thus the way that you and I See things is completely incompatible; There is no one place in the universe Where both of us could reside. And so it is you who must leave, And go wherever you might. The teachings on incompatibility in Buddhism outline two types.  One is a case where one thing cannot be another, since their very identities are mutually contradictory.  Something cannot be in constant flux, for example, and at the same time be never-changing. The second kind of incompatibility is where two things cannot be in the same place at the same time; say, hot and cold.  The classic, amusing example here since ancient times is the owl and the crow, since they are mortal enemies who will never alight upon the same branch at the same time. Which of these two contradictions applies to the understanding of how the pen comes from seed-pictures, and the misunderstanding that thinks it has always come from its own side?  And which contradiction applies to a pen that came from pictures, and a pen that did not? Sixth Canto 31 Useless Meditations, Whereby the Devil Teaches Us Real Emptiness Meditation The cousin who came for a visit

rows.acip: ,KHYOD KYIS STONG SKAD CI SMRAS KYANG, ,NGA YIS CHOS BRGYAD BTANG NA MNGON, ,NGA DANG KHYOD GNYIS 'DZIN STANGS NI, ,DNGOS 'GAL ZHUGS PA NGA YANG 'DOD, ,LHAN CIG 'GROGS PA'I GNAS MIN NA, ,KHYOD RANG GZHAN DU 'GRO BA'I RIGS,
rows.wylie: khyod kyis stong skad ci smras kyang, ,nga yis chos brgyad btang na mngon, ,nga dang khyod gnyis 'dzin stangs ni, ,dngos 'gal zhugs pa nga yang 'dod, ,lhan cig 'grogs pa'i gnas min na, ,khyod rang gzhan du 'gro ba'i rigs
rows.english: You chatter on about emptiness, But it's me who actually takes action, Sending forth all eight of the thoughts. I would also agree That the way that you see things And the way I see them Are completely incompatible; This mind is not a place Where you and I could live together— If you were the one to leave then, That would be best of all. The eight thoughts here would typically apply to what are called the “eight worldly attitudes.”  These are (1) being happy when we get something we want, and (2) unhappy when we don't; (3) happy when we feel good, and (4) unhappy when we don't; (5) happy when people say nice things about us, and (6) unhappy when they don't; (7) happy when they praise us to our face, and (8) unhappy when they criticize us. The Devil is making the point that—if all of us were really able to stay aware that all these things are coming from our own seed-pictures—we would free ourselves from these swings of emotion and simply devote our whole time to planting better seeds, by being nicer to other people. There is a way, incidentally, where we could interpret the “eight” of the verse here as applying to the famous opening prostration in the grandparent of all emptiness teachings: Arya Nagarjuna's famed Wisdom: I bow down To those highest ones, To the totally enlightened ones, The teachers Who showed us how To put to rest The 24 elaborations, And taught the truth Of interdependence: (1) Nothing stops, And (2) nothing starts; (3) Nothing discontinues, (4) Nothing las

rows.acip: ,NGA DANG 'DZIN STANGS MI 'GAL BAS, ,KHYOD NYID BSGOM PAR MI 'GYUR ZHING, ,NGA LA GNOD PAR GA LA 'GYUR, ,DER YANG KHYOD KYIS MA SLEB BO,
rows.wylie: nga dang 'dzin stangs mi 'gal bas, ,khyod nyid bsgom par mi 'gyur zhing, ,nga la gnod par ga la 'gyur, ,der yang khyod kyis ma sleb bo
rows.english: The way they see things then In no way contradicts The way in which I see them. Thus they can't be meditating on you— So how could they do any damage to me? In fact I can't recall that I've met you In a mind in this meditation. The sad irony of the situation is that so many sincere meditators have wasted their time just trying to observe how thoughts rise and disappear, without reflecting upon where they came from: how we treat our fellow beings. Useless Meditation #2 The Trap of Emptying the Mind

rows.acip: ,LA LAS SEMS NI GZUGS CAN DU, ,BTZAL BAS MA RNYED DE BSGOM PA, ,DE NI NGA YI PHYOGS NA'ANG MED, ,'DZIN STANGS 'GAL BA LTA CI SMOS, ,KHYOD KYI PHYOGS NA'ANG MI 'DUG PAS, ,NGA LA CI'I PHYIR GNOD PA BYED,
rows.wylie: la las sems ni gzugs can du, ,btsal bas ma rnyed de bsgom pa, ,de ni nga yi phyogs na'ang med, ,'dzin stangs 'gal ba lta ci smos, ,khyod kyi phyogs na'ang mi 'dug pas, ,nga la ci'i phyir gnod pa byed
rows.english: Some go on an exploration To see if the mind is a physical thing; They discover then that it is not, And think this is some meditation. They're nowhere near me, Much less incompatible With the way I think things are. They're nowhere near you either— How then could they hurt me? Perceiving that the mind is not a physical reality—discovering that what it is and how it is are not the simple result of chemicals moving around—is not to understand the emptiness of that mind. For that, we have to dig down to the seed-pictures and the seeds they are bursting out of, moment to moment.  And there must always be a moral component: the seeds and the pictures they produce come from how I have treated other people. Useless Meditation #4 The Myth of the Naked Mind

rows.acip: ,LA LA RIG PA ZANG THAL ZER, ,SNANG BA YID LA MI BYED CING, ,BSGOM PA YID LA MI BYED BSGOM, ,DES KYANG NGA LA GTAN MI GNOD, ,NGA DANG 'DZIN STANGS 'GAL BA YI, ,GNYEN PO PHYOGS NA'ANG MI GDA' NA, ,KHYOD NYID BSGOM PAR GA LA 'GYUR, ,DER YANG KHYOD KYIS SLEB PA MED,
rows.wylie: la la rig pa zang thal zer, ,snang ba yid la mi byed cing, ,bsgom pa yid la mi byed bsgom, ,des kyang nga la gtan mi gnod, ,nga dang 'dzin stangs 'gal ba yi, ,gnyen po phyogs na'ang mi gda' na, ,khyod nyid bsgom par ga la 'gyur, ,der yang khyod kyis sleb pa med
rows.english: Some do a meditation that they call “The unstoppable mind”; They bring no image at all to the mind, And make no attempt at meditation— Which for them then is meditation. This is another of those meditations That does nothing at all to stop me; It's nothing even close to an antidote, A state of mind which considers things In a way that contradicts the way That I tend to view them myself. It has nothing to do with meditating Upon yourself, and again I can say I've never met you in their minds. Here the Devil reveals the secret of a mental antidote: an accurate state of mind which cannot coexist with another state of mind which in its turn must therefore be mistaken.  That is, if there is an opinion about how to meditate on emptiness which we are unable to hold in our mind as we think about the pen as coming from us—from our ethical seeds—then that opinion has to be mistaken. rows.english: Some do an analysis On the fact that things Are neither one nor many, And again find nothing's there. But what they think To themselves then Is that there is no I, Because it is nothing more Than something labeled with a name; And then they meditate on that. This though is a meditation On what a thing is not; It is not a meditation Upon its very absence— And it's not therefore a thing Which directly contradicts The way that I see things. If there were an elephant in the room where we're sitting right now, we would most likely have noticed it.  But this is even more the case if somebody asks us, “Is there a purple elephant in the room right now—a purple elephant with two heads?” Since there's no such thing in the first place, we would hardly have to look around the room to confirm that the elephant wasn't there, before we answer in the negative. It's not enough only to see that “me” is something that exists through seed-pictures; we need to go further and recognize that there's no “me” here that could exist any other way—independent of such pictures.

rows.english: How on earth can you imagine That you could expel me from this mind Unless you found a viewpoint Which stood in direct opposition To the way that I see things? How could you ever meditate Upon wisdom so long as you Had yet to inflict any damage on me? The concept of one idea “damaging” another is a common and intriguing concept in the study of emptiness.  It just means that we can't possibly think of any particular object in one way and then also think of it in a way that is incompatible with the first. We can't think of something as all blue and then in the same moment think of it as all red.  The one perception “damages” the other. rows.english: I am in fact the easiest thing You could ever have to think about; Still, some people make the claim That they will drive me from their mind. They use the analysis Of the seven types of logic To come to the realization That the “me” you see When you look at your body & mind Was never something real. And then, they say, They will maintain This way of thinking, And stay in a stream Of that realization. The seven types of logic are not being questioned here; only the state of mind which examines them, without an awareness that this state itself “feels” as though it were coming from its own side, and not from pictures flying out of our seeds. The seven refer to the objects we are examining, to determine whether they come from their own side or not.  Those are composed first of all of the five classical parts to the person: physical form; feelings; capacity of discrimination; other factors that compose the individual; and then finally overall consciousness. These five are what in modern times we refer to simply as “body & mind.”  Mind in the five has been broken down into things like feelings and discrimination, since these two are the root of all trouble in the world: I like this or that, I like her or him; because they make me feel good, or not. To the examination of these five we then add an inquiry into whether the simple collection of the five itself is coming “towards” us from the other side; and the same for the physical outline of ourselves.

rows.english: And suppose you say “Space is that blue thing That we can see When we look straight up.” The blue of our sky though Is just the reflection Of color from Mount Supreme, And has nothing to do at all With the meaning of “empty space.” To say that thinking In terms of this kind of space Would in any way disprove me— Much less directly contradict The way I look at things— Is nothing but a joke. True emptiness is similar to empty space in the sense of a place which is absent of physical objects, although in the case of emptiness we are talking about an absence of anything which could exist without flowing from karmic seeds inside our mind. Again, a physical sort of space can refer to the place between the chair and the table; or even to the lack of physical obstruction which allows the chair alone to stand where it stands.  In the parlance of the everyday world, “space” can also refer to the ebony void of outer space, sprinkled with the jewel lights of individual stars. For the ancients, the simple blue void directly above us was the most basic form of space.  Again, our planet was pictured as a tremendous, flat disk with a towering mountain peak in the middle.  This peak was seen as composed of a different gemstone material in each of the four directions. Our planet Earth was perceived as a continent standing in a vast ocean to the south of this central peak.  The culture they were enveloped in taught people that the reason the sky over our continent is blue is that it was reflect

rows.english: If what you're describing Is sustained thoughts of understanding, Then it can be nothing except A meditation on me! Sheesh McGeesh! How can you say It stands opposed To the way that I see things? Suppose we reach a good understanding of empty space, as the absence of any physical obstruction.  It's not emptiness, but at least it's similar in the sense of being the fact that something is not there.  Except in the case of empty space, what's missing is something that could have been there: a chair, or a building. What's missing in the case of existential emptiness is something that never could have existed in the first place—a self-existent entity: a car accident that happened because someone turned left too soon, rather than a car accident that happened because I did someone a minor harm at some point in the past, and failed to cleanse myself of that karmic seed through a sincere act of confession to another person. A meditation upon physical space has the further problem of reinforcing my habit of misunderstanding things.  In any single moment not involved with understanding how nothing exists except through picture-seeds, we are planting new seeds to be ignorant of seeds. “Sheesh McGeesh!” is an important expression of frustration from the Arizona area of the United States, from about 1952. Useless Meditation #25 Meditating On an Impossible Continuation of the Absence of the Impossible

rows.english: Now how does a person Use the power of Quietude To do a meditation On you, my dearest Wisdom, In a way that will work In opposition to The way that I see things? For that they will need To dwell in states Of examination That are truly special— And for that, They will need Attain a pliancy In their capacity To meditate. Without these then How on earth Could they ever expect To reach the meditative State that we call “Insight”? We've already met—above, in verse 164—the two powerful tools known as “quietude” and “insight.”  Briefly put, these are—respectively—a mighty ability to focus the mind in meditation free of the extremes of mental dullness and agitation; while at the same time seeing into the true workings of mental seeds and their resulting pictures in our reality. “Pliancy” in the art of developing meditation refers to a well-practiced ability to tell our own mind what we want it to do—sort of like a well-trained, pet dog.  This skill is often compared by traditional meditation teachers to an acrobat who has an extraordinary level of control over their body as they jump and flip from one trapeze swing to another. And there's a favorite meditation exercise we can use to get there, called “skipping.”  This is where purposely leap—mentally—between differing depths of focus, just to strengthen the mind's capacity.

rows.english: And besides all those, We see some masters Who pull out the reasoning Which says that things Are neither one nor many. They use it then To check and check, And even as they Focus their meditation, Their mind begins to tire— Which means that The power of their ability To maintain their focus, And its clarity, Are all of them lost to me. There is a famous emptiness meditation where we conclude that nothing is plural or singular; which would be to say that a group of three apples did not involve any multiple things, or that a single apple sitting there was not one apple. These ideas are of course silly unless we have mentally added the qualification “which come from their own side, and are not products of my seed-pictures.”  Because it is true that three apples which come from their own side are not plural; and one apple which comes from its own side is not single—simply because to be one or to be many, we must be in the first place. If we fail to qualify everything here as we have just done it, then simply sitting quietly and trying to imagine that nothing in the universe could be singular or plural is a useless exercise, and would rightly wear us out mentally, after only a few minutes of trying.

rows.english: Once other states Of mind, like dullness And agitation, have Gathered their strength, One would have to Start their meditation Over again from the beginning. But instead they keep up This fabricated attempt To stay in balanced focus. They end up doing Their meditation On nothing more Than the simple fact Of awareness— For they have lost That way of holding things Which serves as a Spiritual antidote. If in a meditation all our time is consumed watching as our mind swings between being too busy and not being lively enough, then by definition we are not focusing on an object of the mind, but rather on the mind as an object—and an object which was never the emptiness we were trying to focus on. rows.english: If a fire and some wood Never touch each other, Then how can the fire Burn the wood? It's the same With myself, And the antidote for me. If the ways we view things Never collide, Then not only Can it do me no harm, It actually helps me expand. And then you need not Trouble yourself. A serious fire breaks out in your kitchen, and you run to grab handfuls of a few marbles each to throw on it; which of course has nothing to do with helping a fire or helping put a fire out. If in our meditation on emptiness we never even approach the idea that things are coming from our past behavior, then that emptiness meditation is uniquely useless—since it has nothing to do with what is causing the fire, or what could put it out.

rows.english: And if you say You are maintaining A divine pride Where that pride Does not engage In emptiness, Then its relationship To that emptiness Must be as though it were A detached observer. And then— Since this would not Be a meditation Where I was absent— It would not fit the sense Of two ways of Looking at things that Contradicted each other. Can the Devil and the Angel truly coexist in the same mind—can they both be present there in the same moment—if their opinions of how things exist are so entirely incompatible? It seems reasonable that during an active understanding that nothing is coming from its own side, the Devil would have to retreat to someplace in the mind below our overt consciousness. But simply from the fact that a person who has seen emptiness directly can in less focused moments still feel that things are coming from their own side, we can say that incompatible opinions can nonetheless float together around different parts of the sea of a single mind.

rows.english: A person who meditates On the idea that nothing Exists at all May perhaps have heard, In the beginningless string Of all their previous lifetimes, A single mention of how Nothing has any Nature of its own; And they may have experienced, On some single occasion In the distant past, A meditation upon that. rows.wylie: bdag nyid de ni nga'o zhes, ,nga rgyal de yi 'dzin stangs ni, ,med dgag tsam gyi gsal ngar dang, ,shugs ldan drag la grims pa yi, ,rgyun la mnyam par bzhag nas ni, ,byings rgod med par skyongs shig go
rows.english: And the way in which The pride holds its object Is to say, “I am The combination Of the two”; we maintain A strong sense of detail With nothing more than A simple absence of things. And so you must Be sure to maintain A meditation where You stay in deepest focus— Free of dullness & agitation— Concentrating fiercely. "Combination of the two here"—aside from the propitious connection to the Janis Joplin song—refers to the inseparable joining of emptiness and great bliss.  In states of intense pleasure even among normal people, the inner winds or prana are strong and free, which facilitates the thoughts that always ride upon these winds as we undertake any kind of reflection or focus. We are using the state of bliss to gaze into the emptiness, and we are working to maintain a sense of identification with the joining of these two: "This is who I am." Dullness and agitation are—again—the two great forces that can disturb meditation.  These two then also represent a disturbance of our inner winds, causing them to flow erratically.  This then prevents us from focusing; in this case, upon emptiness.

We don't even need To talk about things Like the lightning bolt; A person could even Just simply meditate On that heavenly body Of a world to stand on And those who stand Upon it.  Even that Would be enough To provide an antidote Which contradicts The way that you Hold to things to be. All along in this last section here, we've been utilizing a technique from the secret teachings of the Diamond Way in Buddhism, where we follow the step-by-step dissolving of an image that resembles a three-section lightning bolt; and as a mnemonic device we associate some idea with the gradual disappearance of each section. And the Angel is saying here that we could just as well have worked with the simple image of a person standing on the floor right in front of us—allowing the parts of them which are not coming from us to drop away, one by one. rows.english: Suppose someone comes along and makes the following claim: Let's consider the perception which holds that sound is an unchanging thing. Isn't it the case that the object it holds to does exist? Why do you say that? Because it does have an object which it is focusing upon.

rows.acip: MA KHYAB NA KHYAB PA YOD PAR THAL, SGRA RTAG PAR 'DZIN PA'I RTOG PA DANG, SGRA MI RTAG PAR RTOGS PA'I RJES DPAG GNYIS DMIGS PA GCIG LA DMIGS NAS 'DZIN STANGS DNGOS 'GAL DU ZHUGS PA'I BLO YIN PA'I PHYIR,
rows.wylie: ma khyab na khyab pa yod par thal, sgra rtag par 'dzin pa'i rtog pa dang, sgra mi rtag par rtogs pa'i rjes dpag gnyis dmigs pa gcig la dmigs nas 'dzin stangs dngos 'gal du zhugs pa'i blo yin pa'i phyir
rows.english: Just because something is the object that the deductive realization that sound is a changing thing is focusing upon doesn't mean that it has to be the object that the perception which holds that sound is an unchanging thing is focusing upon. Suppose you do say that one doesn't imply the other. And yet it does, because the perception which holds that sound is an unchanging thing, and the deductive realization that sound is a changing thing, are both states of mind that focus upon the same object, and hold it in manners which are in direct contradiction. 10 If a Perception Holds to an Object, Is That an Object Which It Believes In?

rows.acip: RGYU MTSAN DE NYID KYIS NA, NGA RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA LTA BU'I DGAG BYA ZHE PHUG LA BZHAG NAS MED MED SNYAM PA'I MED DGAG GI 'DZIN STANGS NYID SKYONG BA YIN NO, ,ZHES GSUNGS PA LTAR BYA'O,,
rows.wylie: rgyu mtshan de nyid kyis na, nga rang bzhin gyis grub pa lta bu'i dgag bya zhe phug la bzhag nas med med snyam pa'i med dgag gi 'dzin stangs nyid skyong ba yin no, ,zhes gsungs pa ltar bya'o
rows.english: For this one reason, then, they can take a version of themselves which does for example exist through some nature of its own and set it deep down there in the center of their heart, as that very thing that emptiness seeks to deny. And then they can review, over and over again, how this version of themselves could never, ever, exist. This then is how they should conduct their actual practice of emptiness. And this then is how we ourselves should put all these ideas into actual practice!

rows.acip: 'DZIN STANGS ZHEN DU SONG NA, RIGS PA DRAN TZAM BYAS TE, SNANG TSUL DE LTAR DU GRUB PA MED MED SNYAM DU BSAM ZHING SKYUR NAS BSGOM PAR BYA LA,
rows.wylie: 'dzin stangs zhen du song na, rigs pa dran tsam byas te, snang tshul de ltar du grub pa med med snyam du bsam zhing skyur nas bsgom par bya la
rows.english: When you start sliding into believing in things again, then give yourself just a small reminder. Come back to thinking about how none of these things could ever, ever, possibly exist in this way that they appear to. Continue meditating and practicing this way, where you throw those mistaken beliefs away from you.

rows.acip: DES NA YID NGOR RGYAL BA'I SKU LTA BU MDUN DU GSAL 'DEBS PA DE NI DMIGS PA YIN, DE LA MI G-YENG BAR 'DZIN STANGS DAM SPRING NGE BAS 'DZIN CING, DMIGS PA DE KHO NA 'CHAR BAR BYED PA DGOS,
rows.wylie: des na yid ngor rgyal ba'i sku lta bu mdun du gsal 'debs pa de ni dmigs pa yin, de la mi g-yeng bar 'dzin stangs dam spring nge bas 'dzin cing, dmigs pa de kho na 'char bar byed pa dgos
rows.english: To summarize, we can say that we are focusing on the object when we are maintaining—in front of us, in front of the mind—this visualization of something like the holy body of a victorious Buddha. We need to reach a point where the way we are holding on to this meditation object is tight as glue, and the mind is no longer wandering off elsewhere. We are only allowing the object of meditation to continue appearing inside of our mind. 3) Dullness & agitation

rows.acip: BYING BA LA PHRA RAGS GNYIS LAS, DMIGS RTEN DRAN PAS ZIN PA NA, GNAS CHA YOD KYANG GSAL CHA MED PA NI RAGS PA DANG, DMIGS PA'I 'DZIN STANGS MA SHOR BA'I GNAS CHA DANG GSAL CHA YOD KYANG, 'DZIN STANGS KYI SHUGS LHOD NAS GSAL CHA'I NGAR MED PA NI BYING BA PHRA MO STE, SGOM BYED PA'I GEGS KYI GTZO BO 'DI YIN,
rows.wylie: bying ba la phra rags gnyis las, dmigs rten dran pas zin pa na, gnas cha yod kyang gsal cha med pa ni rags pa dang, dmigs pa'i 'dzin stangs ma shor ba'i gnas cha dang gsal cha yod kyang, 'dzin stangs kyi shugs lhod nas gsal cha'i ngar med pa ni bying ba phra mo ste, sgom byed pa'i gegs kyi gtso bo 'di yin
rows.english: Dullness, in turn, comes in two types: subtle and gross. The gross form is where we do have some fixation on the object of meditation, but no clarity. Subtle dullness is where we actually do have both fixation and clarity on the object—it hasn't slipped from our grasp—but the strength of our fixation has dropped a bit, and there's no intensity to the clarity. This single state of mind is the one greatest obstacle to successful meditation.

rows.wylie: rang re bla ma zhig la rgyun du spyir dad pa yod kyang ha cang shugs drag cig med pa la, nam zhig skabs skabs su de las lhag pa'i dad pa ngam ngam shugs drag po re skye ba na 'dzin stangs snga ma las grim du song ba ste, de gnyis la khyad yod pa bzhin no
rows.english: Or you could put it like this. We might have a Lama in our life that—generally speaking—we feel faith for; but where the intensity of that faith is not particularly high. And then from time to time in the relationship something happens to make us feel faith which is stronger than usual—almost overwhelming. In this case we can say that the strength of our grip on “the object” has suddenly gotten stronger than before—there is a considerable difference between the two.

rows.acip: DES NA PHOR PA'I JA BZUNG BA NA LAG PAS ZIN PA DANG, DAM POR BZUNG BA DANG, DE YANG YO 'KHYOGS SU SONG MA SONG MIG GIS BRTAGS PA BZHIN, DRAN PAS DMIGS RTEN ZIN TE 'DZIN STANGS DAM POR BYED, SHES BZHIN GYIS BYING RGOD BYUNG MA BYUNG BRTAGS NAS DMIGS PA SKYONG DGOS, SHES BZHIN NI SHES RAB KYI CHAR GTOGS PA YIN,
rows.wylie: des na phor pa'i ja bzung ba na lag pas zin pa dang, dam por bzung ba dang, de yang yo 'khyogs su song ma song mig gis brtags pa bzhin, dran pas dmigs rten zin te 'dzin stangs dam por byed, shes bzhin gyis bying rgod byung ma byung brtags nas dmigs pa skyong dgos, shes bzhin ni shes rab kyi char gtogs pa yin
rows.english: We can go back to the example of holding a bowl of tea in your hand: you need to keep a good grasp on it, and you also have to look at it from time to time to see whether it's still upright, or else tilted to one side or the other. The ability to keep your mind on the meditation object is the hand here that's holding on tightly; whereas watchfulness is checking to see whether or not dullness or agitation have started. Together, they are helping us maintain the object. The mental state of watchfulness, incidentally, is actually considered one form of the mental function of wisdom. 4) Failing to take action

rows.acip: GSAL CHA'I NGAR MED PA'I BYING BA PHRA MO DE SKYES NA THUN GROL BA DANG DMIGS PA BTANG MI DGOS PAR SEMS KYI 'DZIN STANGS GRIM DU BTANG BAS CHOG

rows.english: This means that subtle dullness has arrived—and there is no intensity to the mental clarity. It's not that, at this point, we need to break off our meditation session, or drop the focus on our meditation object. It's sufficient, rather, if we simply tune up our concentration: how tightly we are holding to that object.

rows.english: When we do decide to tighten down this way, there's a chance that as we continue on we will lose the intensity of our clarity—in which case we get a feeling in the mind where the way we hold on to the meditation object is not so clear anymore: it's almost as if the mind is deconstructing. If we are not able to remove this problem, then the gross form of agitation has arrived. As the Essence of the Middle Way puts it: When the vision is too great, And the mind is a touch depressed, Then you should definitely Open up the meditation a bit.

This in itself is the matchless personal advice of the great meditators of the past—keep it in your heart.

rows.acip: DE LTAR BSGOM PA NA GNAS CHA BYUNG NA BYING BA DANG THAG NYE RU SONG BAS BYING ZON BYAS NAS GSAL CHA DANG, 'DZIN STANGS DAM DU DAM DU BTANG, GSAL CHA BYUNG NA RGOD PA DANG NYE BAS RGOD ZON BYAS NAS GNAS CHA BTZAL,

rows.english: As you continue with this meditation, you will reach fixation—which unfortunately might bring you closer to mental dullness. Be on guard for the arrival of the dullness, gradually tuning up your clarity and tightening, in tiny steps, your hold on the object. When you do arrive at clarity, that will bring you close to mental agitation. Now stay on your guard against the agitation, and go for fixation.

rows.english: You can see then that a person can look like they're making some efforts in spiritual practice, but without any real understanding of what the meditative focus they're looking for looks like. You and I shouldn't go this way—rather, we definitely have to try to achieve a kind of meditative concentration which is complete in two different aspects. Generally, there should be fixation; and, more especially, clarity—both characterized by a firm hold on the object.

rows.english: And yet still further—wouldn't it then be wrong to say that one could undertake multiple actions at the same time? Why do you say that? Because it never happens that multiple states of consciousness holding their objects in ways that are not the same could ever occur at the same time.  That is, it would be impossible—in one and the same moment—to have an awareness focused upon a narrow path ahead as part of the outer world; along with an awareness focused upon the specific spot on that path where you were putting your feet; and another awareness where you were thinking “I am me”; and yet another awareness focused upon the earth and rocks belonging to the path before you.

rows.english: The "me " that this state of mind is taking as the object it thinks it sees is the object that we deny: the object that we have to work to deny.  We have to strive to actually see the way this tendency works, face-to-face, inside of our own minds--and not just through some general understanding that we glean from what someone else has told us, or through trying to imagine what the words for it mean.  This entire process then is the first of the four crucial points: we call it "the crucial point of actually seeing how the very thing we deny appears within our mind. "

rows.english: The point then is that--whenever we engage in a visualization practice--we must utilize the deep practice where the profound and the apparent sides of reality are both present. The object appearing to the mind at this same point then is the Angel: the world of the Angel, and all the holy beings inhabiting this world.

rows.english: When we are studying the way of the perfections, we learn that the thing we wish to purify ourselves of and the thing we use to purify ourselves of it are opposed to each other.  That is, the path we are using--the wisdom which realizes that nothing has any self nature--perceives objects in a way which is in direct contradiction with the way they are perceived by our normal tendency to grasp to some self nature.  The wisdom then purifies us of this tendency to grasp at things as if they truly existed.

rows.acip: NGES NGOR RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PA ZHES NGES NGO'I 'DZIN STANGS RANG BZHIN GYIS MED PAR NGES PA'I STONG NYID BSGOM,

rows.english: We speak next of "the object that your perceptions grasp, the fact that nothing has any natural existence."  This refers to the way in which your perceptions hold things to exist: your perceptions grasp that they have no nature in and of themselves; you are meditating on the emptiness of things.

rows.acip: 'DZIN STANGS CHOS THAMS CAD RANG BZHIN GYIS GRUB PA RDUL TZAM YANG MED PA'I STONG NYID KYI LTA BA DBU MA THAL 'GYUR BA, DE LTAR RTOGS MKHAN GYI BLO YANG 'BRAS DUS KYI YE SHES CHOS SKU DNGOS YIN SNYAM PA'I NGA RGYAL TE CHOS SKU'I NGA RGYAL 'JOG PA'I RGYU BZHI TSANG BA DGOS SO,
rows.wylie: 'dzin stangs chos thams cad rang bzhin gyis grub pa rdul tsam yang med pa'i stong nyid kyi lta ba dbu ma thal 'gyur ba, de ltar rtogs mkhan gyi blo yang 'bras dus kyi ye shes chos sku dngos yin snyam pa'i nga rgyal te chos sku'i nga rgyal 'jog pa'i rgyu bzhi tshang ba dgos so
rows.english: How do we interpret these things?  We are maintaining (3) the viewpoint of the Consequence group of the Middle-Way School: the idea of emptiness itself, where there does not exist even a single thing in the universe which possesses a single atom its own nature. Finally we maintain (4) a certain sense of divine pride, where we think to ourselves that this state of mind, this state of realization, is the actual Wisdom Dharma Body of a person at the point of the final goal.  All four of these features must be present.

rows.english: And more especially, in the Way of the Pure, we have the deep practice of inseparable depth and clarity.  Picturing yourself clearly in the form of an Angel acts as a cause for you to achieve the ultimate result of widespread activities [first 3 1/2 perfections]--which is the physical body of the Buddha.  Thinking of Her as having no quality of Her own is a meditation on emptiness, which acts as a cause for achieving goal of the deep side of things--which is the Dharma Body.

rows.acip: 'DI DAG GI SKABS SU ZAB GSAL GNYIS SU MED PA'I RNAL 'BYOR BSKYED RIM GYI SMIN BYED KHYAD PAR CAN DU 'GYUR TE, RNAM PA LHA LA DMIGS PA NI GSAL BA GZUGS SKU SGRUB BYED DANG, 'DZIN STANGS RANG BZHIN MED PAR ZAB PA CHOS SKU SGRUB BYED DANG, DE LTA BU'I NGA RGYAL GSAL SNANG YOD PA NI THABS SHES GNYIS MED KYI RNAL 'BYOR PA YIN LA, DE MIN RDZUN TE SNGAGS KYI SBOM PO 'BYUNG NGO,,
rows.wylie: 'di dag gi skabs su zab gsal gnyis su med pa'i rnal 'byor bskyed rim gyi smin byed khyad par can du 'gyur te, rnam pa lha la dmigs pa ni gsal ba gzugs sku sgrub byed dang, 'dzin stangs rang bzhin med par zab pa chos sku sgrub byed dang, de lta bu'i nga rgyal gsal snang yod pa ni thabs shes gnyis med kyi rnal 'byor pa yin la, de min rdzun te sngags kyi sbom po 'byung ngo
rows.english: Maintaining what we call the "yoga of indivisible depth and clarity" at points like this acts as a powerful force for bringing your practice of the stage of creation to its final ripening.  Seeing yourself in the form of the Goddess functions to bring you the Form Body of a Buddha: which is what the "clarity" in the name of the yoga refers to.  Maintaining a certain perception as you do so -- that is, holding that nothing here has any nature of its own -- functions to bring you the Dharma Body of a Buddha: the "depth" in the name of the yoga.

rows.wylie: 'dzin stangs chos thams cad rang gi blos btags pa tsam las rang ngos nas bden par grub pa rdul tsam yang med par nges pa'i yul can bde ba chen po dang yul stong pa nyid gnyis gnyis snang phra mos kyang bar ma chod par chu la chu bzhag pa bzhin du gyur pa dang
rows.english: Third, how we interpret the object is that every existing thing is nothing more than a label created by our own mind--there is not even an atom's worth of ultimate existence from its own side. The greatest bliss is our subject state of mind, and emptiness is its object.  And this pair of subject and object become like water poured into water--they are unable to be divided, even in a subtle form, into an appearance as two.

rows.acip: DANG PO NI, SNGAR BSHAD PA LTAR BDAG MED PA'I DE KHO NA NYID KYI DON MTHAR THUG PA'I GO BA 'TSOL LUGS LA PHAR PHYIN GYI THEG PA LAS LHAG PA CIG SNGAGS LA MED DE, BDEN 'DZIN GYIS BZUNG BA'I ZHEN YUL RIGS PAS PHU DAG PAR BKAG PA'I SGO NAS BDEN 'DZIN GYI DMIGS GTAD MA BSHIG PAR YID NANG DU BSDUS PA TZAM GYIS NI, BDEN 'DZIN DANG 'DZIN STANGS 'GAL BA MED PAS BDEN 'DZIN LA CI YANG MI GNOD PA'I PHYIR DANG,
rows.wylie: dang po ni, sngar bshad pa ltar bdag med pa'i de kho na nyid kyi don mthar thug pa'i go ba 'tshol lugs la phar phyin gyi theg pa las lhag pa cig sngags la med de, bden 'dzin gyis bzung ba'i zhen yul rigs pas phu dag par bkag pa'i sgo nas bden 'dzin gyi dmigs gtad ma bshig par yid nang du bsdus pa tsam gyis ni, bden 'dzin dang 'dzin stangs 'gal ba med pas bden 'dzin la ci yang mi gnod pa'i phyir dang
rows.english: Here is the first.  As we explained before, it's not the case that here in the way of the secret word there is some form of the understanding of the ultimate reality of suchness--of the fact that nothing is itself--which is somehow superior to that found in the way of the open teachings of the perfections. That is, suppose that we are unable to demolish the way in which our tendency to think things are real holds things to be--suppose that we fail to use reasoning to deny, perfectly, the object which this tendency thinks it sees.  Suppose we simply gather the mind inward. In this case the way our own mind holds things to be will in no way contradict the way our tendency to see things as real holds them to be; and we will have done nothing at all to impede this tendency.

rows.acip: SNANG BA GSUM GYI DUS SU SNANG NGOR DKAR, DMAR, GNAG PA'I SNANG BA 'BYUNG YANG, NGES NGOR SNANG BA DE YANG BKAG NAS STONG NYID 'DZIN STANGS KYI YUL DU BYAS TE, RTZE GCIG TU SGOM PAR BYED PA YIN NO,,
rows.wylie: snang ba gsum gyi dus su snang ngor dkar, dmar, gnag pa'i snang ba 'byung yang, nges ngor snang ba de yang bkag nas stong nyid 'dzin stangs kyi yul du byas te, rtse gcig tu sgom par byed pa yin no
rows.english: At the point where we go through the three visions, what appears to our perceptions are visions of whiteness, redness, and blackness.  When we have stopped these visions from appearing to our perceptions, then we take emptiness as the object as we take it to be.  And then we remain in single-pointed meditation upon it.

rows.acip: BDAG CAG RNAMS LA BKA' DRIN KHYAD PAR DU 'PHAGS PA MKHAS SHING GRUB PA RNYED PA RJE BTZUN MKHAS GRUB BSTAN PA DAR RGYAS DPAL BZANG POS DE LTAR GSUNGS PA GANG ZHIGKHS LEN DGOS YIN PA'I PHYIR,
rows.wylie: bdag cag rnams la bka' drin khyad par du 'phags pa mkhas shing grub pa rnyed pa rje btsun mkhas grub bstan pa dar rgyas dpal bzang pos de ltar gsungs pa gang zhigkhs len dgos yin pa'i phyir
rows.english: And he did so speak it be this way, because he did so in his Overview of the Perfection of Wisdom, with the following words: "When we use 'something which is made' as a reason to prove that sound is a changing thing."
